author: Plutarch
note: Primary narrative source. Written ~130 years after Antony's death. Plutarch draws on lost earlier sources including memoirs and Augustan-era accounts. Some passages likely incorporate anti-Antonian propaganda.

author: Appian of Alexandria
note: Detailed narrative of Roman civil wars from the Gracchi to Actium. Books 3–5 cover the Second Triumvirate and conflict with Octavian. Draws on sources hostile to Antony.

author: Cassius Dio
note: Most complete continuous narrative of the period. Books 41–51 cover Caesar's civil war through Actium and Cleopatra's death. Heavily influenced by Augustan tradition.

author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
note: Fourteen speeches delivered against Antony after Caesar's assassination. Contemporary hostile source by Antony's political enemy. Essential for 44–43 BCE period.

author: Gaius Julius Caesar
note: Caesar's first-person account of the civil war 49–48 BCE. Mentions Antony's role at Pharsalus and as tribune. Contemporary but self-serving.

author: Suetonius
note: Biography of Augustus with coverage of the conflict with Antony. Draws on Augustan-era sources including Augustus' own memoirs.

author: Augustus
note: Augustus' first-person funerary inscription listing his achievements. References the war against Antony and Cleopatra. Propaganda but contemporary.

author: Various
note: Coins issued by Antony and the triumvirs provide contemporary visual evidence. Includes legionary denarii (32–31 BCE) and Cleopatra portrait coins.

author: C.B.R. Pelling
title_en: Plutarch: Life of Antony (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics)
note: Definitive modern commentary on Plutarch's Life of Antony. Critical analysis of Plutarch's sources, biases, and historical accuracy.

author: Adrian Goldsworthy
note: Modern scholarly biography combining literary sources, archaeology, and military history. Strives to separate Augustan propaganda from historical fact.

author: Ronald Syme
note: Foundational study of the transition from Republic to Principate. Influential analysis of Antony as a Caesarian leader. Classic but Augustan-skeptical perspective.
